newsitem.title: DENMARK: Cheering Danes hear Clinton praise their country.
newsitem.headline: Cheering Danes hear Clinton praise their country.

text.p: Thousands of cheering Danes heard U.S. President Bill Clinton on Saturday thank their country for its peacekeeping troops and praise their efforts to help the Baltic states as a contribution to European peace.

Clinton, on the first visit to Scandinavia by a serving U.S. president, lauded moves by Denmark to help integrate the Baltics -- former Soviet republics Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia -- in a joint peacekeeping battalion and to boost trade.

"I thank Denmark for rising to this moment, especially for reaching out to Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, helping them to fortify their economies, establish the Baltic Battalion and take their place in the new Europe," he said.
"By bridging the expanse of the Baltic Sea you are closing a gap in history."

Clinton got a tumultuous welcome at a rally in Copenhagen's central Nytorv square that featured jazz and rock bands and a choir. Police said the crowd packed in and around the 17th century square and watching from windows numbered 80,000.
Denmark has championed the former Soviet Baltic republics in their bid to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) and the European Union.
The three small nations won their independence in 1991 and see NATO membership as a measure of permanent protection.
The Madrid summit of NATO leaders invited only the Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland into the alliance, although they mentioned the Baltic states as aspiring members.
Clinton also praised Denmark's contribution to international peacekeeping forces in Bosnia and elsewhere.

"Denmark provides more peacekeepers proportionally than any other nation. You were among the first to heed Bosnia's call. Despite the loss of brave Danish soldiers while the war raged you have never wavered," Clinton said.
"For your unshakable commitment to peace --- and for all you do -- I have come here to say on behalf of the American people: Thank you," he added.
Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen returned the praise, saying that without U.S. reconstruction aid after World War II Europe would not have been able to grow as it did.
In remarks to reporters at Copenhagen international airport after the U.S. president's departure for Washingtoin, he said Clinton's tumultuous welcome reflected the affection in which Danes held him.
"It is not every day that Danes have the opportunity to spontaneously express their positive feelings for a political leader," he said.

"It is a great privilege in one's political work when the president of the United States visits Denmark for the first time in its history ...I am very moved by this and happy with the political cooperation we enjoy."
After speaking, Clinton walked along a rope barrier cordoning off the V.I.P. area from spectators and shook hands with wellwishers.
Clinton arrived on Friday, had talks with Rasmussen and stayed overnight at the summer palace of Queen Margrethe.
